overview: Puerto Rico’s history includes knowledge passed through hands, families and neighbourhoods. Hammock makers work plant fibres, coffee farmers teach younger growers, and dancers exchange ideas with drummers. These living practices belong to an island shaped by Indigenous, African and European histories and a wider Puerto Rican diaspora.

periods.title: Indigenous ceremonial communities
periods.summary: Caguana’s courts and carved stones belong to a late precolonial ceremonial centre. This approximate phase highlights one site, not the first settlement or a single island-wide state.

periods.title: European contact before Spanish settlement
periods.summary: Columbus reached Puerto Rico in 1493. Spanish colonial settlement followed in 1508; Indigenous life had a much longer history.

periods.title: Spanish colonial rule
periods.summary: Spanish colonial institutions reshaped the island. San Juan became a fortified port; its expanding walls and forts survive as evidence of centuries of colonial engineering.

periods.title: Abolition with restrictions
periods.summary: The 1873 abolition law ended slavery while imposing compulsory labour contracts on freed people.

periods.title: United States military government
periods.summary: U.S. forces invaded during the 1898 war. Spain ceded Puerto Rico in the Treaty of Paris; military government preceded civilian administration.

periods.title: Civilian territorial government
periods.summary: The Foraker Act established civilian government in 1900, with an appointed governor and an elected legislative chamber.

periods.title: Citizenship and territorial institutions
periods.summary: The Jones-Shafroth Act granted U.S. citizenship in 1917 and established a locally elected bicameral legislature. Federal control remained.

periods.title: Commonwealth constitutional government
periods.summary: Puerto Rico adopted its own constitution in 1952. The commonwealth remained a U.S. territory.

sections.title: Discoveries: spaces for gathering and living

items.text: At Caguana in Utuado, a ceremonial centre dating broadly to 1200 to 1500 CE, excavators uncovered rows of limestone slabs around a levelled plaza. Some bore carved faces. Builders cut into the hillside to create the flat gathering space. The remains show organised construction and a setting for communal ceremonies, although every activity cannot be reconstructed from the stones alone.

Between two of Caguana’s courts, excavators recorded postholes outlining a circular wooden building, along with two hearths, decorated pottery and a carved stone cemí, a spiritual object. A piece of Spanish glazed pottery appeared with Taíno objects in an undisturbed context. This association suggests activity into the contact period, rather than a perfectly clean break between two worlds.

Smithsonian researchers documented an elderly Puerto Rican woman making hammocks with fibres from the maguey plant. Textile specialist Soraya Serra Collazo helped the team find this living craft tradition. Turning a tough plant into a place to rest takes considerable skill. A good nap can begin with somebody else’s hard work.

The builders of Castillo San Cristóbal designed the fort to collect rain. Five cisterns beneath its plaza stored water for use inside. Those underground reservoirs were part of the engineering that made the eighteenth-century fortress workable. Beneath the impressive courtyard lay a practical answer to a very ordinary problem: everyone gets thirsty.

A January 1942 photograph by Jack Delano shows children outside a wooden building in Aibonito. Above the doorway, the sign reads “Comedor Escolar,” meaning school dining room. Open shutters and a corrugated roof are visible. School history includes places to eat as well as classrooms, although this photograph does not tell us what lunch tasted like.

In the early twentieth century, Bailey Ashford and Pedro Gutiérrez worked on Puerto Rico’s hookworm problem. Their programme combined investigation and treatment with teaching about infection and improving waste disposal to reduce contact with contaminated soil. The historical account shows that caring for health extended beyond a doctor’s consulting room into public facilities and everyday surroundings.

In a 2022 interview, filmmaker Russell Oliver described learning about farming at Hacienda Masini in the mountains of Yauco. He met older coffee farmers who wanted to pass their knowledge to the next generation. His team’s documentation project grew from those relationships. Behind a cup of coffee are people learning about plants, land and the work of growing a crop.

In bomba, the lead drummer responds to a dancer’s movements, turning gestures into rhythms. Your feet can give the drummer homework. Singing often uses call and response, while barrel-shaped drums, a maraca and wooden sticks contribute different sounds. The tradition developed among African-descended communities in Puerto Rico and continues through performances and workshops on the island and in its diaspora.

Margarita “Tata” Cepeda’s bomba dress entered the story told by the Smithsonian’s Latino museum in its 2023 exhibition rotation. The museum connects the garment to the Cepeda family’s work performing and teaching bomba and plena. Clothing can preserve a history of movement and family learning, as well as fabric and colour.

Puerto Rico’s March 22, 1873 abolition law declared an end to slavery, yet required freed people to enter labour contracts lasting at least three years. Former enslavers received compensation, while full political rights for the freed people were delayed. The law’s clauses show why a legal declaration of freedom did not immediately remove every coercive restriction on daily life.

Voters approved a Puerto Rican constitution in 1952, followed by congressional approval. It organised the island’s internal government, including elected leaders and courts. Constitutional self-government and independent national sovereignty are different things: Puerto Rico continued within the United States territorial system.

Caguana is also a place of living spiritual meaning. In a 2007 account, Taíno advocates described their campaign for ceremonial access and a voice in caring for the site, including a 2005 protest. Their perspective reminds us that an archaeological park can be someone’s sacred place. Present-day communities have their own knowledge, responsibilities and views about its future.

ending.text: Spanish rule ended in 1898, followed by United States administration and later commonwealth government. Puerto Rico remains a U.S. territory. Its communities and Indigenous heritage continue through changing institutions and cultural practices.
